title: Much Ado About Nothing
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Messina, in and around Leonato's house, over about a week
lengthNote: Around 2,500 lines, the greater part of them in prose
openingLine: I learn in this letter that Don Peter of Arragon comes this night to Messina.
summary: Two couples are made by the same method. Beatrice and Benedick are talked into love by friends who arrange for them to overhear flattering lies; Claudio is talked out of it by a stranger at a window. The play's comedy and its near-catastrophe run on identical machinery, and it takes a pair of incompetent constables to notice the difference.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Much Ado About Nothing
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Placed by its style and by the company's records at the end of the 1590s.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The First Quarto, printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise and William Aspley.

atAGlance.label: Source tradition
atAGlance.note: The Hero plot belongs to a European story family found in Ariosto and in Bandello; Beatrice and Benedick are Shakespeare's own.

atAGlance.label: Title
atAGlance.note: The two words sounded close in early modern English, and almost every turn of the plot depends on somebody noting — watching, overhearing or reporting.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The soldiers’ return, and Claudio falls for Hero
structure.summary: Don Pedro's company returns from a war that cost almost nothing, and the house fills with young men with time on their hands. Claudio decides within minutes that he loves Hero; Beatrice and Benedick resume a quarrel that predates the play; and Don John, newly and unconvincingly reconciled to his brother, announces that he would rather be disliked than pretend.

scenes.title: The messenger
scenes.summary: Beatrice asks after Benedick before he arrives; Claudio asks Don Pedro to court Hero for him.

scenes.title: Half a rumour
scenes.summary: Antonio brings Leonato a garbled report that the prince loves Hero himself.

scenes.title: Plain-dealing villain
scenes.summary: Don John states his character outright and begins looking for something to spoil.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The masked dance, and the gulling of Benedick
structure.summary: At the masked ball the wooing is done by proxy and briefly believed to be a betrayal. Once that is cleared up, Don Pedro proposes the only labour of Hercules he thinks worth attempting: getting Beatrice and Benedick to admit they like each other. The gulling of Benedick, staged in an orchard, works within a dozen lines.

scenes.title: The masque
scenes.summary: Beatrice abuses Benedick to his masked face; Claudio believes briefly that Don Pedro has taken Hero for himself.

scenes.title: Borachio's offer
scenes.summary: Don John is told how a window, a borrowed name and a willing servant can wreck the match.

scenes.title: Benedick in the arbour
scenes.summary: A song, then three men loudly discussing Beatrice's hopeless love, and a bachelor converted.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Beatrice gulled, and Don John’s deception
structure.summary: Hero and Ursula play the same trick on Beatrice, and it works even faster because it accuses her of pride, not weakness. Meanwhile Don John shows Claudio a scene at a window, and the watch — half asleep and entirely illiterate in the ways of their betters — arrest the two men who staged it.

scenes.title: Beatrice in the garden
scenes.summary: She overhears herself described as too scornful to be loved, and surrenders in rhyme.

scenes.title: A changed Benedick
scenes.summary: His friends mock his shaved beard and perfume; Don John invites Claudio to see proof.

scenes.title: The watch
scenes.summary: Dogberry instructs his men to avoid trouble, and they arrest Borachio bragging about the deception.

scenes.title: Dressing
scenes.summary: Hero's women joke about husbands and heaviness on the morning of the wedding.

scenes.title: Too late
scenes.summary: Dogberry tries to tell Leonato what his watch has found and is sent away to hold the examination himself.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Hero accused at the wedding
structure.summary: Claudio waits until the ceremony to denounce Hero: this is a plan, not an outburst. She faints, her father believes the accusers, and a friar proposes to report her dead. Left alone in the empty church, Beatrice and Benedick admit they love each other, and she immediately asks him to kill his best friend.

scenes.title: The church
scenes.summary: The public shaming, the swoon, the Friar's plan, and 'Kill Claudio'.

scenes.title: The examination
scenes.summary: Dogberry conducts an inquiry he cannot follow and gets the confession anyway.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Grief, confession and a second wedding
structure.summary: Leonato challenges the men who broke his daughter, and is laughed at for being old. The truth comes out through the constables’ paperwork, not the gentlemen’s investigation. Claudio mourns at a tomb, agrees to marry a cousin sight unseen, and is given Hero back.

scenes.title: Old men and swords
scenes.summary: Leonato and Antonio challenge Claudio and Don Pedro; Benedick does the same in earnest; Borachio confesses.

scenes.title: Bad verses
scenes.summary: Benedick tries to write a love poem, fails, and learns Hero is cleared.

scenes.title: The monument
scenes.summary: Claudio reads an epitaph and hangs a scroll on a tomb that contains nobody.

scenes.title: The masked brides
scenes.summary: Hero unmasks, the lovers are caught out by their own handwriting, and Don John is reported taken.

characters.name: Beatrice
characters.summary: She has the fastest tongue in Shakespearean comedy and uses it, by her own admission, as armour: the play hints at an earlier hurt from Benedick that she will not describe. Her anger after the wedding is the point at which the comedy nearly stops being one.
characters.clue: She would rather hear her dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves her, and her first request of the man she finally admits loving is that he kill his friend.

characters.name: Benedick
characters.role: A lord of Padua, of Don Pedro's company
characters.summary: His anti-marriage act is loud enough to be a performance, and the gulling scene works by letting him surrender without losing face. He is the only man in the play who takes Beatrice's account of the wedding seriously, and he changes sides for her at real cost.
characters.clue: He swears he will die a bachelor, is talked out of it by three friends shouting in a garden, and ends up challenging his commander's favourite.

characters.name: Hero
characters.summary: She speaks little in the first half and is discussed constantly, which is precisely what makes her vulnerable: her reputation exists entirely in other people's mouths. In 3.1 she runs the trick that catches Beatrice, so the play does show her capable of managing a scene when she is given one.
characters.clue: Her value is agreed by everyone before she has said fifty words, and it is destroyed in public by a man who never asks her a question.

relationships.label: betrothed to, denounced by, married to

characters.name: Claudio
characters.summary: He falls in love by report, asks another man to do his courting, and believes an accusation on the evidence of a window at night. His cruelty at the wedding is a rehearsed public performance, not hot temper, and the play makes him accept a wife sight unseen before it forgives him.
characters.clue: He never speaks to the woman he loves without an intermediary, and he saves his accusation until the altar so that everybody can hear it.
traits: conventional to the point of cruelty

characters.name: Don Pedro
characters.summary: He arranges everything: Claudio's marriage, the gulling of two friends, and, without meaning to, the conditions in which a lie about Hero can be believed. He ends the play with no partner and one line of consolation offered to him, which several productions have made the quietest moment in the last scene.
characters.clue: He courts one woman on another man's behalf, invents the plot that marries two enemies, and is left standing alone at the end of it.

characters.name: Don John
characters.summary: He announces that he is a villain in his third scene and offers no reason beyond his position, which is the interesting thing about him: a defeated bastard brother in a household where legitimacy is everything. He needs to invent almost nothing, because the men around him are ready to believe it.
characters.clue: He calls himself a plain-dealing villain and says he is trusted with a muzzle; his whole plot amounts to arranging for two people to be seen at a window.

characters.name: Leonato
characters.summary: Hospitable, pleased with his household, and the first person in the church to believe the accusation against his own daughter. His grief in 5.1 produces the best serious verse in the play, and it is directed at the men who wronged her only after a friar has told him she is innocent.
characters.clue: He welcomes a prince, gives away a daughter, and at the altar wishes aloud that somebody would lend him a dagger.

characters.name: Dogberry
characters.summary: He reverses almost every word he uses and is right about almost every fact. The play's crime is solved by men the gentry cannot be bothered to listen to, and the running joke about being written down an ass carries a real grievance about who is believed.
characters.clue: He tells his watchmen to let thieves go sooner than risk a scuffle, and then demands to be written down, on record, as an ass.

relationships.label: tries and fails to report to

characters.name: Margaret
characters.summary: She stands at the window in her mistress's clothes and is the physical cause of the catastrophe, and the play excuses her in a line and a half without asking what she thought she was doing. Her bawdy jokes on the wedding morning are the last cheerful thing said before the church scene.
characters.clue: She wears her mistress's gown at a window one night, and the play forgives her in half a sentence without ever letting her explain.

themes.name: Noting, overhearing and evidence
themes.summary: Nobody in this play learns anything by being told it directly. Information arrives by eavesdropping, by report, by a scene arranged for a particular watcher, and the play's title puns on the word for it. Both love plots and the slander plot use exactly the same device, which is the argument the comedy is making.
themes.development: Two staged overhearings in Act II and Act III produce a marriage; a third staged sight in Act III nearly produces a death.

themes.name: Reputation and public honour
themes.summary: Hero's worth is established by other people's praise and destroyed by other people's testimony; she is never asked to give an account of herself until it is too late to matter. Messina is a small enough world for a name to be the whole of a person's estate.
themes.development: The accusation is deliberately staged at the altar, and the repair is staged there too — the second wedding is as public as the first because the damage was.

themes.name: Wit
themes.summary: Beatrice and Benedick talk brilliantly in order not to be caught out, and the friends who trick them understand this exactly: both are given permission to love by being told they are already loved. Wit in this play is protective clothing, and the plot works by removing it.
themes.development: Their prose skirmishing in 1.1 becomes rhymed resolve in 3.1, awkward confession in 4.1, and a scrap of bad poetry produced as evidence in 5.4.

themes.name: Men and women
themes.summary: Beatrice’s fury in the church is that manhood has melted into courtesy: the men have the swords and the credit, and they use both to destroy a girl. ‘Kill Claudio’ puts the question of whether a man’s loyalty to another man can be outweighed by his loyalty to the truth.
themes.development: Benedick does not answer at once: he says no first, then agrees, and the challenge he eventually delivers is spoken quietly and in prose.

themes.name: Benign and malicious deception
themes.summary: The play does not draw a clean line between a kind lie and a cruel one. Don Pedro's trick is a gift and Don John's is an attack, but both rely on the target's existing self-image, and both work because being watched makes people believe what they are shown.
themes.development: The Friar’s plan in 4.1 is a third kind: a false report used to cancel the effect of another false report.

themes.name: Repair
themes.summary: The comedy ends with the right people married and the villain caught, but Shakespeare does not pretend the wedding scene never happened. Claudio is given a penance, not an argument, and Hero’s first words to him afterwards correct him about who she is.
themes.development: The tomb scene, the second veiled bride and Benedick's call for a dance are three separate attempts to close the play, and the last one has to talk over Don John's arrest.

techniques.name: Prose as the main medium
techniques.definition: Unmetred speech carrying the substance of a play, not just its low comedy.
techniques.inThisBook: Most of the play is prose, and the lovers' most important exchanges are in it; verse arrives for ceremony, grief and the moment Beatrice surrenders in rhyme at the end of 3.1.

techniques.name: Eavesdropping
techniques.definition: A scene performed by characters who know they are being overheard, for a listener who thinks he is not seen.
techniques.inThisBook: Shakespeare builds the same scene twice, once for each lover, and gives the audience the pleasure of watching a performance and its dupe at the same time.

techniques.name: Malapropism
techniques.definition: Using a word that sounds like the intended one and means something else, usually the opposite.
techniques.inThisBook: Dogberry's comparisons are odorous and his suspects are full of piety; the joke works because the errors keep accidentally telling the truth about Messina.

techniques.name: The pun on nothing and noting
techniques.definition: A double meaning carried by two words that sounded almost identical in early modern English.
techniques.inThisBook: The title names both the fuss over a non-event and the play's real mechanism, observation; the same pun runs through Balthasar's scene about musical notes in 2.3.

techniques.name: Offstage action
techniques.definition: Withholding the decisive action from the audience and showing only its report.
techniques.inThisBook: The window scene that ruins Hero is never staged; the audience hears it planned and hears it described, which puts them alongside the watch and not alongside Claudio.

techniques.name: Song as commentary
techniques.definition: A lyric that states the play's theme from outside the action.
techniques.inThisBook: Balthasar's 'Sigh no more, ladies' advises women to expect men to be deceivers, and it is sung to distract Benedick immediately before he is deceived.

quotations.text: There is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her: they never meet but there's a skirmish of wit between them.
quotations.speaker: Leonato
quotations.context: Explaining Beatrice to the messenger, who has just heard her insult a man she claims not to care about.
quotations.analysis: The phrase frames the relationship as a spectacle the household enjoys, which is exactly why the two of them cannot drop it: an audience is watching. Note that it is the uncle who supplies the label, before either of them is on stage together — their love is a matter of public commentary before it is a matter of feeling.

quotations.text: What, my dear Lady Disdain! are you yet living?
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: His first words to Beatrice in the play, after she has interrupted him.
quotations.analysis: He greets her with an allegorical title, as though she were a figure in a morality play, and she takes the personification off him in her reply and feeds it. Neither of them uses the other's name in this whole exchange, which is the shape of the defence they have both agreed to.

quotations.text: I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Agreeing, competitively, with Benedick's claim that he loves no woman.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is precise: both are noise made by a creature that does not mean anything by it. She says this in front of her uncle and a room of guests, which makes it a position she will have to be seen to abandon — and the friends who trick her know it.

quotations.text: Can the world buy such a jewel?
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Asking Benedick what he thinks of Hero, minutes after arriving in Messina.
quotations.analysis: Benedick has just asked whether he means to buy her, and Claudio's answer accepts the vocabulary without noticing it. He values Hero as a possession whose worth is set by general agreement, which is why a general agreement that she is worthless can destroy her in one scene.

quotations.text: it must not be denied but I am a plain-dealing villain. I am trusted with a muzzle and enfranchised with a clog;
quotations.speaker: Don John
quotations.context: To Conrade, who has advised him to look more cheerful now that he is reconciled to his brother.
quotations.analysis: He claims the one virtue available to him — not pretending — and describes his pardon as a muzzle and a chained block. The imagery is of a dangerous animal on a lead, and it is his own; the play gives him no motive beyond the position his birth has left him in.

quotations.text: Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more, Men were deceivers ever, One foot in sea and one on shore, To one thing constant never:
quotations.speaker: Balthasar
quotations.context: The song sung in Leonato's orchard while Benedick hides in the arbour.
quotations.analysis: The song tells women to stop grieving over men who are unreliable by nature, and it is performed as cover for three men about to tell an elaborate lie. Its advice is also the play's plot in advance: Claudio will be exactly the deceiver described, and the ladies will be told to let him go.

quotations.text: No, the world must be peopled. When I said I would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I were married.
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Alone in the orchard, immediately after the gulling.
quotations.analysis: He reverses a public vow in two sentences and gives a reason of cosmic scale for a decision of purely private appetite. The joke in the second sentence is a genuine piece of self-knowledge dressed as a quibble: he did not expect to live long enough to be caught out, and he has been.

quotations.text: Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu! No glory lives behind the back of such. And, Benedick, love on; I will requite thee, Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand:
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Coming forward after overhearing Hero and Ursula discuss her pride.
quotations.analysis: She surrenders in rhymed verse, the only time she speaks it, and the metrical shift does the work a soliloquy would do elsewhere. The falconry image — a wild bird taken to the hand — is one she chooses herself, and it concedes rather more than the trick actually asked for.

quotations.text: Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
quotations.speaker: Hero
quotations.context: The closing line of the scene in which she and Ursula trap Beatrice.
quotations.analysis: Hero, who is usually spoken about and seldom speaks, gets the couplet that names the play’s method. A trap is not an arrow: it requires planning, bait and a victim who walks in, and every match in Messina is made that way, including the one that goes wrong.

quotations.text: Comparisons are odorous: palabras, neighbour Verges.
quotations.speaker: Dogberry
quotations.context: Trying to tell Leonato what his watch has arrested, on the morning of the wedding.
quotations.analysis: He means odious, and the mistake is funnier than the word he wanted; but the scene is also the play's most painful piece of timing, because Leonato is in a hurry and sends him away. The catastrophe of Act IV is entirely preventable, and it is prevented by nobody because of who is speaking.

quotations.text: O, what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: In the church, beginning the accusation, having so far refused to say the word 'marry'.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation is about men, not about Hero, and it is the nearest the scene comes to self-knowledge: what men dare do is precisely what Claudio is about to do to a girl in front of her father. The line breaks off mid-sentence, and the completed thought never arrives.

quotations.text: Give not this rotten orange to your friend; She's but the sign and semblance of her honour.
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Handing Hero back to Leonato at the altar.
quotations.analysis: The image is of fruit that looks sound and is rotten inside, and it makes a person damaged goods being returned to a supplier. ‘Sign and semblance’ is the play’s own subject stated by its worst reader of signs: Claudio has believed a semblance, and he is accusing her of being one.

quotations.text: But fare thee well, most foul, most fair! farewell, Thou pure impiety and impious purity!
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: His last words to Hero before she faints.
quotations.analysis: Two lines of perfectly balanced antithesis produced by a man in what he presents as uncontrollable grief — the rhetoric is far too neat for the emotion it claims. Shakespeare gives him the figure twice over, with the nouns and adjectives swapped in the second half, so that the speech sounds composed in advance, because it was.

quotations.text: I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that strange?
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Alone with Beatrice in the empty church after Hero has been carried out.
quotations.analysis: The declaration arrives in the wreckage of somebody else's wedding, and he ends it with a question because he cannot say it without a shrug. 'Nothing' is the title word, and here it is doing honest work for once: he loves nothing so well, in a play where nothing has been the cause of all the trouble.

quotations.text: Kill Claudio.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Her answer when Benedick tells her to bid him do anything for her.
quotations.analysis: Two words, immediately after a page of elaborate prose, and the shortest speech either of them makes in the play. It is the point where the comedy's machinery — a lover offering extravagant service — is taken literally, and the audience's laughter, which almost always comes, is part of what the scene is testing.

quotations.text: O God, that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the market-place.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Explaining to Benedick why Claudio is her enemy.
quotations.analysis: She says it three times in twenty lines, which is a measure of how completely her wit has failed her. 'In the market-place' is the detail that matters: Hero was destroyed in public, so the revenge Beatrice imagines is public too, and it has to be carried out by a man because the law and the sword both belong to men.

quotations.text: But manhood is melted into courtesies, valour into compliment, and men are only turned into tongue, and trim ones too
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, on the men of Messina.
quotations.analysis: It is a complaint about talk from the play's best talker, and it convicts her own weapon: wit is what the men have instead of action. The verbs are all of liquefaction and exchange — melted, turned — as though a substance had been swapped for a currency.

quotations.text: O that he were here to write me down an ass! But, masters, remember that I am an ass; though it be not written down, yet forget not that I am an ass.
quotations.speaker: Dogberry
quotations.context: In the prison, having been called an ass by Conrade during the examination.
quotations.analysis: His grievance is that the insult has not been entered in the record, and the joke is that he insists on the record being complete even when it damns him. Messina has just ruined a girl on unwritten testimony; the constable is the only person in the play who believes that what is said should be written down.

quotations.text: For there was never yet philosopher That could endure the toothache patiently,
quotations.speaker: Leonato
quotations.context: Refusing his brother's advice to bear his daughter's disgrace calmly.
quotations.analysis: He answers moral consolation with dentistry, and the deflation is the point: the men who counsel patience have not been in the chair. It is the best serious writing in the play, and it is given to the man who, one scene earlier, wished his daughter dead sooner than shamed.

quotations.text: Done to death by slanderous tongues Was the Hero that here lies:
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Reading the epitaph at Leonato's monument, believing Hero dead.
quotations.analysis: The penance is a poem, hung on a tomb containing nobody, read by the man whose tongue did most of the slandering — and the epitaph does not name him. Shakespeare gives the scene formal rhymed stanzas and a ritual, which is either the repair Messina needs or an exact measure of how cheap its rituals are.

quotations.text: for man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion.
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Explaining why nobody should mock him for marrying after swearing he never would.
quotations.analysis: He does not defend the reversal; he generalises it into a fact about the species and calls that a conclusion. It is the play's answer to its own machinery — people are talked into things, and the sensible response is to marry, dance, and not examine it too closely.

timeline.label: Ariosto's Orlando Furioso first published
timeline.detail: Its story of Ginevra, falsely accused after a maid is seen at her window in her mistress's clothes, is the closest analogue to the Hero plot.

timeline.label: Bandello's Novelle
timeline.detail: Another version of the slandered bride, set in Messina, which brings the story to the city Shakespeare uses.

timeline.label: Sir John Harington translates Orlando Furioso
timeline.detail: The English verse translation makes the Ginevra episode available to readers and playwrights in London.

timeline.label: The play is most likely written
timeline.detail: Composition is usually placed in 1598 or 1599, at the end of the decade of comedies.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise and William Aspley; its title page links the play to the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

timeline.label: Performed at court
timeline.detail: Recorded among the plays given during the celebrations for the marriage of Princess Elizabeth.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, with some of the quarto's confusing speech prefixes regularised.

timeline.label: Peggy Ashcroft and John Gielgud at Stratford
timeline.detail: The pairing that began the modern tradition of the play as a vehicle for two major actors.

timeline.label: Judi Dench and Donald Sinden for the RSC
timeline.detail: One of the best remembered of the company's many Beatrice and Benedick pairings.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh's film
timeline.detail: Shot at the Villa Vignamaggio in Tuscany, with Emma Thompson as Beatrice; one of the most commercially successful Shakespeare films.

timeline.label: Iqbal Khan sets the play in contemporary Delhi
timeline.detail: An RSC production with Meera Syal as Beatrice, staged as part of the World Shakespeare Festival.

timeline.label: Kenny Leon's Public Theater production is filmed
timeline.detail: An all-Black cast in a contemporary American political setting, recorded for broadcast.

places.name: Messina
places.note: The whole play: Leonato's house, its orchard and garden, a church and a prison.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Benedick's city, named in the first scene along with the reputation that precedes him.

places.name: Florence
places.note: Claudio's city; the first scene introduces him as a young Florentine who has fought beyond the promise of his age.

places.name: Zaragoza
places.note: Chief city of Aragon, the kingdom Don Pedro is prince of and the source of the company's rank.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the 1600 quarto was printed and where the Lord Chamberlain's Men first played it.

criticalViews.position: The play belongs to Beatrice and Benedick
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the inherited slandered-bride plot is the frame and the invented couple are the picture: the comedy's real subject is two intelligent people arguing themselves out of a defence.
criticalViews.counter: It leaves Act IV hard to account for, since the church scene is the longest and most serious writing in the play and Hero is at the centre of it.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long noticed that nothing here is learned first-hand. The same technique, a scene staged for a watcher, makes one marriage and nearly destroys another, which makes the play an argument about how societies decide what is true.
criticalViews.counter: The resolution comes from a confession, not from anybody reasoning better, so the play may be less confident about evidence than the reading suggests.

criticalViews.position: A play about what men are permitted to do
criticalViews.summary: Recent stage practice and criticism have concentrated on Claudio's public shaming of Hero, Leonato's readiness to believe it, and Beatrice's fury that revenge is a man's office. The second wedding leaves the comedy open.
criticalViews.counter: Hero herself is given no scene in which to judge Claudio, which makes it difficult to say what the play thinks the right ending would be.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use deception in Much Ado About Nothing?
essayQuestions.focus: Overhearing, evidence and the two plots
plan: Establish the pattern: nobody in this play learns anything except by watching or being told.
Compare the two gulling scenes, 2.3 and 3.1, and note that each accuses its target of the fault they most fear.
Set Don John's window scene against them, and observe that Shakespeare never stages it.
Add the Friar's false report of Hero's death as a third kind of lie, used as medicine.
Conclude on the watch: the truth arrives from the people nobody bothered to listen to in 3.5.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Beatrice.
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, anger and the limits of comedy
plan: Begin with 1.1, where she asks after Benedick before admitting she has any interest in him.
Read her wit as defence, not temperament, using her hint at an earlier hurt.
Use the rhymed verse of 3.1.113 to show how completely the trick works, and how much she concedes in the image of the tamed bird.
Turn to 4.1: the repeated wish to be a man, and the demand that Benedick act because she cannot.
Close by asking whether the last scene's discovered sonnet restores the comedy or simply puts the armour back on.

essayQuestions.question: Is Claudio forgivable?
essayQuestions.focus: Reputation, repentance and the second wedding
plan: Note how he falls in love: by report, through a proxy, with a woman he has spoken to scarcely at all.
Show that the denunciation at 4.1.29 is staged, not impulsive: he waits for the altar and an audience.
Weigh the mourning of 5.3 against the fact that he agrees to marry an unseen cousin the next morning.
Consider what the play withholds: Hero never accuses him, and no character demands that he explain himself.
Decide whether the comedy asks for forgiveness, or simply moves on and leaves the audience to decide.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Dogberry and the watch?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, language and who gets believed
plan: Set out the joke first: a constable who reverses his words and instructs his men to avoid arresting anyone.
Show that the watch nevertheless overhear the confession that solves the plot, in 3.3.
Make 3.5 the centre of the argument — Leonato is in a hurry and will not listen, and the wedding proceeds.
Read the 'write me down an ass' joke as a grievance about record and testimony as well as a gag.
Conclude on the reversal: the gentlemen read signs badly and the fools take statements accurately.

discussionQuestions: Both love plots are begun by a lie. Does the play think that matters?
Shakespeare never shows the scene at Hero's window. What does the play gain by keeping it offstage?
'Kill Claudio' usually gets a laugh. Should it?
Leonato believes the accusation against his own daughter before anyone else does. Is he forgiven too easily?
Don Pedro ends the play without a partner. What should a production do with him in the final dance?

related.why: The next of the great comedies, and the other one in which a joke played on a self-important man goes too far to be laughed off.
Written within a year or two, and the closest comparison for two people talking themselves into love in prose.
The same accusation of a faithful woman, taken seriously enough to kill a child and to need sixteen years to mend.
The slandered-wife plot again, with the malicious deceiver given a full part and no comic constables to stop him.
Shakespeare's other comedy of people made to love on someone else's instruction, with the trickery done by magic instead of gossip.
